A single-layer network with width $N$ can span a subspace of dimension $N$. Once $N$ exceeds the dimension of the target subspace, the network can represent the function exactly regardless of the number of constraints $w$.

[Hypothesis Index]

The solvability of the bootstrap problem is governed by a phase transition in the loss landscape at a critical width $w_c$. As the constraint count $w$ increases, the network first enters a basin of attraction where gradient descent successfully converges to the zero-violation solution. Below this threshold, the dynamics are trapped in local minima, resulting in a fat regime; crossing it yields a rigid regime where $N_c(w)$ remains constant as $w$ increases.

The violation probability follows a heavy-tailed distribution determined by the data density and network capacity. The minimal width $N_c(w)$ required to achieve zero violation on a test set scales logarithmically with the constraint count $w$, reflecting the statistical difficulty of covering the support of the data distribution as constraints increase.

The function space defined by the bootstrap constraints possesses a manifold structure with a non-trivial topology. The rigid regime corresponds to a region where the manifold is locally flat (Euclidean), allowing a low-dimensional network to approximate it, while the fat regime corresponds to a region of high curvature or topological complexity that requires higher dimensionality to resolve.
